question: The department lists "power law dynamics" in artifact effectiveness. Do the latest citation counts support a power law over simpler alternatives?
production_path: investigation: read the department record, PSY-001, PSY-002, scripts/quality_trend.py and scripts/evolution_metrics.py at the pinned commit, and, after an independent agent review pointed to it, logic/fractal-compounding.md, the specification PSY-001 gives as its first source; found three department strings that name power laws as a topic, a detection rule in the specification (a power law is present when the top 20% of artifacts hold more than 60% of citations) applied to these citation counts, and that 2 of the 18 latest citation counts are hand-typed values for artifacts outside the repository

extract: snapshot the 18 citation counts of the latest run with their sources, citation paths and values before git grep into observed-input.json, refusing any source file whose Git blob differs from the pin

model: discrete power law, discrete exponential and rounded-up lognormal on the same integers, fitted by maximum likelihood above a stated cut; Vuong test on the log-likelihood ratio and Kolmogorov-Smirnov goodness of fit
test: log-log rank line, power-law fits at ten cuts, three-family comparison on the 16 positive counts and power law against exponential on the 12 counts of 13 or more

simulation: 2,000 seeded samples per family at 16 values and tails of 12, 50 and 200 values, for the spread of the exponent, the R squared of the rank line and how often the comparison finds the generating family

adversarial: negative controls, the fit without the two hand-typed counts, the hand-typed counts of 2026-09-13 as a sensitivity case (likelihoods, goodness of fit and the specification's share rule), a recomputation with other libraries outside the repository, and the objection that the result describes the counting instrument
test: byte-identical reruns of the analysis, 46 self-checks, five answered exercises and an answer-free transfer task
hypothesis: The 18 latest citation counts are too few to support a power law: a least-squares line on the log-log rank plot will look acceptable (R squared above 0.8), yet the maximum-likelihood comparison will not favour the power law over an exponential or a lognormal, and synthetic samples of the same size will be assigned to the wrong family in more than one run in five, so that no family can be singled out.
evidence: At Demerzel commit 4b03838800dcd4894f1e026461979bff1d985ca8 the department record names power laws three times (lines 10, 17 and 26) as two research areas and a curriculum entry, with no data set or test, and no line of PSY-001 or PSY-002 uses the term; the specification PSY-001 cites first (logic/fractal-compounding.md, line 56) states a share rule on these counts, a power law being present when the top 20% of artifacts hold more than 60% of citations. By that rule the three or four largest counts held 67.2% or 74.1% of 116 citations on 2026-09-13 (a power law) and hold 40.3% or 51.2% of 414 at the pin (none). The latest quality-trend run (2026-10-13T18:43:54Z) holds 18 citation counts summing to 414: 2 are zeros, 2 are hand-typed values for artifacts outside the repository, and 2 are counted on one shared citation path.

On the 16 positive counts the log-log rank line has slope -1.152 and R squared 0.669, a value that 1,989 of 2,000 synthetic power-law samples of 16 values reach or exceed. An R squared of 0.9 or more occurs in 81.8% of the power-law samples but also in 40.0% of the lognormal and 7.3% of the exponential ones, so a high value would not have identified the family.

Discrete maximum likelihood gives an exponent of 1.297 for all positive counts and 2.21 for the 12 counts of 13 or more, and from 1.297 to 7.602 over ten cuts. Over all positive counts the power law has the lowest log-likelihood (-80.97 against -67.74 for the exponential and -69.93 for the lognormal; Vuong p below 0.0001 and 0.012) and none of 2,000 synthetic power-law samples lies as far from its fit, while on the tail above 13 the power law is neither ruled out (goodness-of-fit p = 0.2505) nor separated from the exponential (log-likelihood ratio -1.71, p = 0.2557); at the cuts 15 and 17 the exponential is favoured with p = 0.0832 and 0.0364, and the cut 13 was chosen after seeing the counts.

In 6,000 synthetic samples of 16 values (the positive counts, not 18) the generating family has the highest likelihood in 3,785 (63.1%), and with 12 tail values a true power law gets a decisive correct verdict against an exponential in 27.0% of samples, against 99.3% with 200 values. The hypothesis is refuted on two points (R squared is 0.669, not above 0.8; one family, the power law, is singled out as excluded over the full range) and holds on two (the comparison does not favour the power law; more than one sample in five is assigned to another family); belief P refers to the lesson's answer, not to the hypothesis.

With the hand-typed counts that the same artifacts carried until 2026-09-13, the same analysis gives R squared 0.959 and no decisive comparison, and the goodness-of-fit p-value is 0.0805, already under 0.1, so the result depends on the counting instrument; the analysis reran byte-identically on Python 3.9, 3.12 and 3.14 under Windows and on Python 3.14 under Linux. When this record was written (2026-10-13), no human subject review, learner trial, translation or publication of this course existed; research duration was not instrumented and duration_seconds=0 records that limitation.
